facts.claim: UNESCO element title, exact: 'Lavash, the preparation, meaning and appearance of traditional bread as an expression of culture in Armenia'. Inscribed in 2014 (9.COM) on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

UNESCO's lavash text says lavash 'plays a ritual role in weddings, where it is placed on the shoulders of newlyweds to bring fertility and prosperity'. (UNESCO wording; paraphrase as UNESCO describes it, e.g. 'laid on the newlyweds' shoulders as a wish for fertility and prosperity'.)

UNESCO's lavash text: preparation is typically done by a small group of women; the dough of wheat flour and water is rolled thin, stretched over an oval cushion and slapped against the wall of a traditional conical clay oven; the group baking strengthens family, community and social ties.
UNESCO element title, exact: 'Duduk and its music'. Inscribed in 2008 (3.COM) on the Representative List, originally proclaimed in 2005.

UNESCO's duduk text says duduk music 'accompanies popular Armenian traditional songs and dances of the various regions and is played at events, such as weddings and funerals'. It is usually played by two musicians, one holding a continuous drone by circular breathing while the other plays the melody.

UNESCO's duduk text: the body is ideally made from apricot wood; there are four major types, 28 to 40 cm long; the 40 cm duduk is regarded as most suited to love songs, the smaller one usually accompanies dances. UNESCO also notes it is played less in popular festivities and more as staged performance by professionals.
UNESCO element title, exact: 'Kochari, traditional group dance'. Inscribed in 2017 (12.COM) on the Representative List. Correct URL ends 01295 (the 01291 URL resolves to Greece's Rebetiko).

UNESCO's Kochari text says it is 'widely performed throughout Armenia during holidays, festive celebrations, family ceremonies and other social events' and is 'open to all participants, irrespective of age, gender or social status'. UNESCO's description text does not say 'wedding' in the body (the page's keyword tags include 'Wedding'); it does not describe how dancers hold hands or shoulders.

Smartraveller Armenia, as at November 2026: overall advice Level 2, 'Exercise a high degree of caution'; Level 4 'Do not travel' within 5 km of Armenia's border with Azerbaijan (mines and unexploded ordnance). Write neutrally, no political framing. Smartraveller CNI page (last updated 1 October 2026): if you're getting married overseas, local authorities may ask you to prove you aren't already married; a Certificate of No Impediment to Marriage (CNI) is a DFAT document issued to support an intended marriage overseas. DFAT issues CNIs through Australian Passport Offices, through Australian embassies, high commissions and consulates overseas, and by mail. At least one applicant must be an Australian citizen or permanent resident.

Smartraveller CNI page: DFAT can't advise on another country's legal processes; couples should ask the destination's embassy in Australia or the local authority responsible for marriage whether a CNI is needed (a Single Status Certificate or No Record Result Certificate from a state or territory registry may be accepted instead), whether it must be issued in that country, and whether it needs an apostille or authentication.

Smartraveller CNI page: the local authority may ask for other documents, such as a birth certificate or a divorce certificate; ask whether these need legalising. DFAT charges fees for CNIs (fees rise with CPI on 1 January each year). No amount is recorded here, per the brief.

insider_details.detail: If you want lavash on your shoulders as a guest-facing moment, plan it at the arrival at the reception or the family home and brief the photographer; UNESCO ties lavash to weddings in exactly this way, so it reads as heritage rather than a gimmick.

UNESCO describes the duduk as usually played by two musicians (a drone and a melody), so book a pair rather than a soloist if you want the traditional sound, and allow for the longer duduk for a slow, romantic piece.
Kochari is open to every age and is danced at family ceremonies, so it works as the moment that gets both grandparents and friends onto the floor; plan floor space for a large group line.

Australia has no mission in Armenia and DFAT says some authorities accept only a CNI issued in-country, so ask the Armenian registry early whether an Australian-issued CNI (or a state registry single status certificate) is accepted, and whether it needs an apostille, before anyone books flights.

For Armenian-Australian couples, remind any dual-national groom and family that Smartraveller says dual nationals must travel on the Armenian passport, and that male dual nationals aged 18 to 28 may be liable for military service; raise it at the first planning call, not at check-in.
Keep wedding events, coach transfers and day trips well away from the 5 km band along the Azerbaijan border that Smartraveller rates Level 4; Yerevan-based plans keep logistics simple.
